title: Partial Derivatives are Slices
tagline: Freeze one variable, take an ordinary derivative — the gradient just collects the slopes
summary: A surface tilts differently in every direction, so it has no single slope. Move a point across a filled contour map of f(x,y) and watch two 1-D slices appear: one holds y fixed, one holds x fixed, and each carries a tangent whose slope is the matching partial derivative. The green gradient arrow stacks the two partials, always pointing uphill and perpendicular to the contours. A bowl, a saddle, and a ripple make critical points, steepest ascent, and the meaning of a zero gradient concrete.
highlights: Drag a point over a filled contour map of a bowl, a saddle, or a ripple and see both slice curves update live.
Each slice draws its own tangent, whose slope is exactly the partial derivative held in one variable.
The gradient arrow collects both partials and always points uphill, at right angles to the contour bands.
Read partial-x, partial-y, gradient norm, and height as four linked numbers.
See why a zero gradient can be a minimum, a maximum, or a saddle — and why -grad is the direction descent steps.
